conflicts.description: Public solenoid 17, the first continuous output, is asserted continuously by the ROM but is not one of the three continuous devices the solenoid identification table lists. PinMAME's LISY bridge treats Centaur's continuous bit 0 as a strobe line and masks it out of the coil data, while by35.c takes the sixth switch-column strobe from PIA1:B bit 7 (public 20) instead. The two readings cannot both be right and the address stays unresolved.

PinMAME keeps a generic flipper-button column at internal column 11, which VPinMAME publishes at 81-88; this is the lower right button position. Centaur declares FLIP_SW(FLIP_L) with no FLIP_SWNO, so FLIP_SWL and FLIP_SWR are both zero and core_updateSw never copies this column into the game switch matrix. The ROM strobes only columns 1-6 and never reads this address. The machine's real flipper buttons are the single matrix address 21, which both retained scripts drive. This entry is retained because the legacy corpus bound it and consumers may still resolve the alias, not because it is a physical contact.

PIA1:B bit 4, the first of the four continuous outputs, and the one continuous output the solenoid identification table does not account for: the printed table lists exactly three continuous devices, at 16, 17 and 18, which are public 18, 19 and 20. The address is certainly driven - in the retained self-test trace it goes high once and is still high in the final snapshot, the only continuous output permanently asserted - so it is not an empty slot, but what it drives is unresolved and the two available sources disagree. PinMAME's LISY bridge special-cases Centaur at src/lisy/lisy35.c case 7, calling lisy35_switch_pic_init(1) for J4 pin 5 and setting lisy35_J4PIN5_is_strobe, after which lisy35_solenoid_handler masks continuous bit 0 out of the coil data with cont_data &= 0x0e; that is this address, and LISY filters it precisely because it is not a coil. Against that, by35.c assembles the sixth switch column for non-Vector games from PIA1:B bit 7, which is public 20, the magnet, not bit 4. The J4-pin to PIA-bit correspondence is inferred from LISY's mask constants rather than from a Bally schematic, so the address stays unresolved rather than being asserted either as unused or as the column strobe. Resolving it needs the solenoid-driver and switch-strobe schematic sheet, or a harness run that watches switch column 6 while this line is toggled. Two independent reviews split on whether this should read as used: the address is demonstrably driven, but if it is the column strobe it is not an output device at all, so the record stays unknown until the by35.c/lisy35.c discrepancy is resolved.

Solenoid identification table entry 16. The ROM's own solenoid self test pulses this coil while displaying 16, which printed page 13 states is the number assigned to the solenoid, so public address 18 and printed number 16 are the same device. The retained v2.0.0 script repurposes this address to drive desktop and VR backglass illumination; that is a table convenience, not the physical device.

Solenoid identification table entry 17. The ROM's own solenoid self test pulses this coil while displaying 17, which printed page 13 states is the number assigned to the solenoid, so public address 19 and printed number 17 are the same device. Energising this relay enables the two flipper coils, which are wired through it rather than to a driver-board output and therefore have no solenoid number of their own. The retained standalone script uses it as the game-on signal for nudge handling.

Solenoid identification table entry 18. The ROM's own solenoid self test pulses this coil while displaying 18, which printed page 13 states is the number assigned to the solenoid, so public address 20 and printed number 18 are the same device.

The right-hand lower flipper coil. Centaur's flipper coils are switched by the K1 relay and the flipper button contacts directly rather than by a solenoid-driver output, so they carry no Self Test number and appear nowhere in the solenoid identification table; the parts list counts them as Flipper (2). PinMAME synthesises public addresses for them anyway - core.h defines sLRFlip as 46 and sLLFlip as 48 - and both retained scripts bind those callbacks. The address is an emulator-side handle on a real coil, not an extra device.

Retained human transcription of every printed table this definition depends on - the solenoid and switch identification tables, the Figure V off-playfield classification, the parts list assembly coils, the self-test to public solenoid reconciliation, and the retained-script callback comparison - together with the rendered PNG page cache under external:pinmame-manuals/rendered/bally.centaur.1981/. The retained PDF is image-only, so every table was read from rendered pages rather than OCR. The transcription carries a correction log: two of its original conclusions were wrong and were corrected after independent review.

sources.locator: Pinned LibPinMAME harness runs that boot centaur from empty NVRAM and step the self-test button into the ROM's solenoid test, which pulses each coil in turn while writing that coil's identification number to the player score displays. Pairing each pulsed public solenoid address with the displayed number yields the printed-to-public mapping for all eighteen coils, repeating identically across four complete cycles. The same runs enumerate 76 lamp addresses, nineteen solenoid addresses and seven display indices.
